Title: Choose Boring Technology
Author: Dan McKinley
Notes:
1. We only have so much room for innovation. Spend it on the actual business problem, not on making every part of the tech stack new.
2. Boring doesn't mean bad. Choose proven tools that are good enough for the job. Their capabilities and failure modes are better understood, so there are fewer unknown surprises.
3. Pick tools for the whole company, not just one task. Every new tool adds operational work and things people need to learn. A tool that works well enough for several problems can be better than a different "best" tool for each one. Keeping the system reliable matters far more in the long run than making it easier to build.
4. Before adding new tech, work out how you'd solve the problem with what you already have. If the real goal is just to try a new tool, stop. Otherwise, write down what makes the current stack too costly or difficult to use, and discuss the choice across the company.
5. New tech is fine when it earns its place. If it overlaps with or replaces something you already use, commit to moving the old functionality over and propose a timeline. The point is to ship and leave room for bigger problems, not collect tools.
